problem: Source names the bird: "if a plover whistled"; modern generalizes to "a bird", losing the specific moorland detail.
new_text: Some time passed before I felt calm even here. I had a vague dread that wild cattle might be nearby, or that some hunter or poacher might discover me. If a gust of wind swept the wasteland, I looked up, fearing it was the charge of a bull; if a plover whistled, I imagined it a man. Finding my fears groundless, however, and soothed by the deep silence that settled as evening gave way to night, I grew more confident. Until now I had not thought; I had only listened, watched, dreaded. Now I regained the ability to reflect.

problem: Source says "without it, it would be difficult to proceed"; modern intensifies to "nearly impossible".
new_text: Around two o'clock I entered the village. At the bottom of its single street there was a little shop with some loaves of bread in the window. I wanted a loaf of bread desperately. With that nourishment I could perhaps recover a degree of energy: without it, it would be difficult to go on. The desire for some strength and vitality returned as soon as I was among other people. I felt it would be degrading to collapse from hunger on the pavement of a hamlet. Did I have anything on me I could trade for one of those rolls? I considered. I had a small silk handkerchief tied around my throat; I had my gloves. I had little idea how men and women in the depths of poverty went about things. I did not know whether either of these items would be accepted: probably they would not; but I had to try.

problem: Source "I was driven to the point now" means she was forced to the moment of decision; "driven to the breaking point" implies collapse, a different sense.
new_text: I thought it over. It had come to the point now. I stood face to face with Necessity. I was someone without a resource, without a friend, without a coin. I had to do something. What? I had to apply somewhere. Where?

problem: Source "Let me condense now" announces that she will summarize the rest briefly (which she then does); "Let me move on" loses that sense.
new_text: Reader, it is not pleasant to dwell on these details. Some say there is satisfaction in looking back on past suffering; but to this day I can barely stand to revisit the times I am describing: the moral humiliation, blended with the physical suffering, forms too painful a memory to willingly revisit. I blamed none of those who turned me away. I felt it was only to be expected, and could not be helped: an ordinary beggar is often regarded with suspicion; a well-dressed beggar, inevitably so. To be sure, what I begged for was work; but whose responsibility was it to give me work? Certainly not the responsibility of people who were seeing me for the first time and knew nothing of my character. And as for the woman who would not take my handkerchief in exchange for bread—well, she was right, if the offer looked suspicious to her or the trade seemed unprofitable. Let me be brief now. I am sick of the subject.

problem: Source "I seemed intimate with every lineament"; modern adds "inexplicable", an interpretive word not in the source.
new_text: A strange place this humble kitchen was for such occupants! Who were they? They could not be the daughters of the elderly woman at the table; she looked like a country woman, and they were all refinement and cultivation. I had never seen faces like theirs: and yet, as I gazed at them, I seemed to know every feature intimately. I cannot call them beautiful—they were too pale and serious for that: as each bent over a book, they looked thoughtful almost to severity. A stand between them supported a second candle and two large volumes, which they consulted frequently, comparing them with the smaller books in their hands, like people using a dictionary to help with translation. The scene was as silent as if all the figures had been shadows and the firelit room a painting: so hushed was it that I could hear the cinders falling from the grate, the clock ticking in its corner; I even thought I could distinguish the click-click of the old woman's knitting needles. When, therefore, a voice broke the strange stillness at last, it was perfectly clear to me.

new_text: "That is powerful," she said when she had finished. "I love it." The other girl, who had lifted her head to listen to her sister, repeated, while she gazed at the fire, a line of what had been read. problem: Source "It isn't likely" (plain refusal in Hannah's register); modern "That's not happening" is anachronistic slang that changes her tone.
new_text: Mistrust—the very reaction I dreaded—appeared in Hannah's face. "I'll give you a piece of bread," she said, after a pause; "but we can't take in a vagrant for the night. It isn't likely."

problem: Source "Who or what speaks?" conveys Jane's fear that the voice may not be human; modern "Who speaks?" drops "or what".
new_text: "Who or what speaks?" I asked, terrified by the unexpected sound, and no longer capable of drawing hope from anything that happened. A figure was near—what figure, the pitch-dark night and my weakened sight prevented me from making out. With a loud, long knock, the newcomer called at the door.

problem: Source "I can fancy her physiognomy would be agreeable" is a modest judgment; "quite attractive" overstates it (and undercuts the later contrast with St. John's "plain").
new_text: "She has a distinctive face; gaunt and hollow as it is, I rather like it; and when she is healthy and animated, I imagine her face would be pleasant."

problem: Source keeps a sustained soil metaphor: prejudices are hard to eradicate "from the heart whose soil has never been loosened or fertilised by education"; modern "a mind that has never been opened" drops the soil image that the following "weeds among stones" depends on.
new_text: It was full of the fragrance of fresh bread and the warmth of a generous fire. Hannah was baking. Prejudices, it is well known, are hardest to uproot from a heart whose soil has never been loosened or enriched by education: they grow there as firmly as weeds among stones. Hannah had been cold and stiff at first: lately she had begun to soften a little; and when she saw me come in tidy and properly dressed, she actually smiled.

problem: Source "will keep me, if but in the barest necessaries of life" — the hedge "if but" (even if only) is dropped.
new_text: "I do need it, and I seek it to this extent, sir: that some truly kind person will point me toward work that I can do, and for which the pay will keep me, if only in the barest necessities of life."

problem: Source "a claim, to a certain extent, on my confidence" means a right to be confided in; "on my honesty" changes the sense. Also the source leaves the quotation open because Jane's speech continues in 29.107; the modern closes it.
new_text: "Mr. Rivers," I said, turning to him and looking at him as directly as he looked at me, "you and your sisters have done me a great service—the greatest one person can do for another: you have rescued me, through your generous hospitality, from death. This gift gives you an unlimited claim on my gratitude, and a claim, to some extent, to be taken into my confidence. I will tell you as much of the history of the wanderer you have sheltered as I can tell without compromising my own peace of mind—my own safety, moral and physical, and that of others.

problem: Source "despise the day of small things" quotes Zechariah 4:10 (fitting for a clergyman); modern "look down on modest beginnings" loses the recognizable scripture.
new_text: "My sisters, you see, take pleasure in keeping you," said Mr. St. John, "as they would take pleasure in keeping and nursing a half-frozen bird that some winter wind might have blown through their window. I feel more inclined to set you on the path to keeping yourself, and shall try to do so; but understand, my world is small. I am merely the minister of a poor country parish: my help must be of the humblest kind. And if you are inclined to despise the day of small things, seek more effective aid than I can offer."
